nameStory: Rock whitlow-mustard gets its name from its preferred rocky habitats and its historical use in treating 'whitlow' — a painful infection around fingernails. The 'mustard' part comes from its membership in the mustard family, whose members often have a sharp, peppery taste. Early herbalists believed this little plant could draw out infections when applied as a poultice.
description: Rock whitlow-mustard is a small, hardy annual plant that rarely grows taller than 6 inches. It forms low rosettes of tiny leaves with delicate white flowers that seem almost too dainty for the harsh rocky places it calls home. This diminutive member of the mustard family is easily overlooked, but once you spot its characteristic four-petaled flowers and see where it grows, you'll start noticing it tucked into rocky crevices throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in a cross shape, typical of mustard family plants. Each flower is only about 1/8 inch across and feels papery to the touch when dried.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves covered in fine star-shaped hairs that give them a grayish-green, fuzzy appearance. Run your finger over them and they feel distinctly velvety and slightly rough.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, compact rosettes that hug the ground, rarely exceeding 6 inches tall. The entire plant has a cushion-like appearance that helps it survive in exposed rocky locations.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, flattened seed pods called silicles that are oval-shaped and contain several tiny seeds. The pods split open when ripe, releasing seeds that rattle softly if you shake a dried plant.

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Almost always found growing directly from cracks in rocks or in very thin, gravelly soil. It seems to thrive where most other plants can't establish themselves.

habitat: Rock whitlow-mustard lives up to its name by preferring rocky outcrops, cliff faces, stone walls, and gravelly areas throughout New England's mountains and hills. You'll find it growing in the thin soil of rock crevices, often on south-facing exposures where the sun beats down mercilessly. It's particularly common on granite and quartzite outcrops in the White Mountains and Green Mountains, where it shares space with other hardy rock-garden specialists.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin flowering in late April to May, taking advantage of cool, moist conditions before summer heat arrives. Look for the small white flower clusters during this peak blooming period.
seasonality.summer: Continues flowering into early summer while producing seed pods. Plants may look stressed and dried during hot, dry periods but often revive with rain.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open, releasing next year's generation. Plants begin to wither and turn brown as they complete their annual lifecycle.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems and empty seed pods may persist, creating small brown tufts in rock crevices. Seeds lie dormant, waiting for spring warmth to germinate.

funFact: Rock whitlow-mustard can actually grow in less than half an inch of soil — it's been found thriving in rock cracks so narrow that you can barely slip a credit card into them, somehow finding enough nutrients and moisture to complete its entire life cycle in these seemingly impossible conditions.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small white-flowered drabas, but rock whitlow-mustard's preference for rocky habitats is the key distinguishing feature — if you find it growing in rich garden soil or woodland areas, it's probably a different species. Remember: 'rock' whitlow-mustard really means rock!
contextualKnowledge: The term 'whitlow' is largely forgotten today, but it once described a common and painful bacterial infection around fingernails. Many plants with 'whitlow' in their names were traditional remedies for this condition, though there's no scientific evidence supporting their effectiveness. Modern gardeners sometimes call these plants 'draba' after their scientific genus name.
compareHints: Rock whitlow-mustard differs from common whitlowgrass by its preference for rocky habitats (common whitlowgrass grows in disturbed soil and gardens) and its more robust, perennial-like appearance. Unlike wood whitlow-grass, which prefers shaded forest clearings, rock whitlow-mustard thrives in full sun on exposed rock faces. The star-shaped hairs on its leaves are also more prominent than on its relatives, giving it a distinctly fuzzy, grayish appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common whitlowgrass differs from its relatives rock whitlow-mustard and wood whitlow-grass primarily by its habitat preferences and timing.
Wood Whitlow-grass differs from Common Whitlow-grass by having more stem leaves and preferring shaded forest habitats instead of sunny, disturbed ground.
